title: How to Spot a Fake Shareholder Register
summary: How to spot a fake shareholder register: edited percentages under the 25% UBO line, cap tables vs. registers, and the checks that catch them.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** A fake shareholder register is a register of members, stock ledger, or cap-table export submitted in KYB whose names or percentages do not match the company's real books, most often edited so that an owner lands just under the 25 percent line in[31 CFR 1010.230](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-X/part-1010/subpart-B/section-1010.230) . Open Ownership documents the pattern at scale: in the Russian Laundromat, which moved a reported USD 20.8 billion, stakes sat at 4.9 percent under a 5 percent rule and dropped to 0.9 percent when the threshold fell to 1 percent. A tidy table with a company seal says nothing about whether the arithmetic is honest.


## What a Fake Shareholder Register Actually Is


A shareholder register is the company's own record of who holds its shares, how many, and of what class. UK law calls it the register of members.[Section 113 of the Companies Act 2006](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/113) requires every company to keep one, with each member's name and address, the date they became a member, the date they ceased to be one, and, for a company with share capital, the shares held by each member, distinguished by number and class, with the amount paid. Delaware calls the same record the stock ledger.[DGCL § 219(c)](https://delcode.delaware.gov/title8/c001/sc07/) defines it as the records in which the names of all stockholders of record, the number of shares registered to each, and all issuances and transfers are recorded, and makes it the only evidence of who may vote at a stockholder meeting.


A cap table is a different object. It is a model of ownership, usually a spreadsheet or a platform export, and it often mixes issued shares with options, warrants, SAFEs, and convertible notes on a fully diluted basis. In a KYB packet, all three arrive under the same label: proof of who owns the applicant and in what percentage.


A fake one makes that ownership claim without being the company's actual record. It comes in two production families. Edited-after-creation starts from a genuine register, a real platform export, or counsel's ledger, then changes a name, a share count, or a percentage. Generated-from-scratch builds the table to a target, so every row sums correctly because the totals were written first. Neither is the company's books.


The motive is almost always the threshold. Under 31 CFR 1010.230, a covered institution must identify each individual who owns 25 percent or more of the equity interests of a legal entity customer, plus one individual with significant responsibility to control or manage it. An owner shown at 24 percent disappears from the first prong.[Open Ownership's analysis of thresholds](https://www.openownership.org/en/publications/beneficial-ownership-in-law-definitions-and-thresholds/thresholds/) notes that any threshold can be exploited by keeping stakes just below the line, and the Russian Laundromat example shows the line moving and the stakes moving with it.[UBO identification](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/what-is-ubo-identification) is the judgment the register is supposed to support, not a replacement for it.


## Tells That Still Work, and the Ones That Don't


No row crosses 25 percent. Aggregate related holders and the group owns almost everything.


The useful tells on a shareholder register are arithmetic and cross-document, not visual. A register is a table of numbers, and numbers have to agree with other numbers the applicant does not control as easily.


Tell What it catches What it misses


Share counts do not sum to issued shares Hand-edited percentages with stale counts A table generated to balance by construction


Issued shares exceed authorized shares in the charter Registers built without reading the articles Fakes that copy the authorized figure correctly


Several holders clustered at 20 to 24.9 percent Ownership split to stay under the 25 percent line Genuine founder splits that happen to land there


Holders sharing an address, surname, or parent entity Related parties who together cross the threshold Nominees with no visible link to the owner


Percentage basis switches between documents Fully diluted figures used to shrink an owner below 25 percent of issued equity Packets that use one basis throughout


No transfer history behind a recent change A holder who appears or shrinks just before onboarding A fabricated transfer row added with it


The basis switch deserves its own sentence. The CDD rule counts equity interests, and a cap table that reports a founder at 22 percent fully diluted may show the same founder above 25 percent of issued shares once unexercised options and unconverted notes come out of the denominator. That is not always fraud. It is always a reason to recompute.


The tells that fail are the ones that look official. A company seal, a "certified true copy" stamp, a director's signature, and a cap-table platform's logo all survive an edit, because the edit happens to the rows and leaves the furniture alone. A screenshot of a cap-table dashboard is the weakest form of all: it has no export history and can be altered in a browser before capture.


A related-party cluster is the most common honest-looking fake. Spouses, adult children, a trust, and a holding company each sit at 15 to 24 percent, and no single row crosses the line. The[FATF guidance on beneficial ownership of legal persons](https://www.fatf-gafi.org/content/dam/fatf-gafi/guidance/Guidance-Beneficial-Ownership-Legal-Persons.pdf) says thresholds should not exceed 25 percent, that countries may consider combined ownership interests such as shareholders working together, and that individuals who exercise ultimate control should be identified regardless of whether their shares exceed any threshold. A clean register can still hide a controller.


## How Detection Actually Works


Detection on a shareholder register reads the file's story, then reconciles its numbers against documents the applicant produced at different times for different reasons.


Production method asks how the file was made. A native export from a cap-table platform, a law firm's ledger printed to PDF, a spreadsheet saved as PDF from an office suite, and a page assembled in a design tool leave different structural traces. A register that claims to be a platform export but carries an office-suite producer string was handled after it left the platform.


Timestamp trail asks whether that history fits the claimed date. Registers change with every transfer, so a recent save is normal. A file saved minutes before upload, with the percentage column as the last edit, is a different story from a ledger that accumulated entries over years.


Issuer matching ties the register to the entity. Legal name, registration number, jurisdiction, and share classes should match the[certificate of incorporation](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/how-to-spot-a-fake-certificate-of-incorporation) or articles, and authorized shares should support the issued total. For an LLC, the member schedule in the[operating agreement](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/how-to-spot-a-fake-operating-agreement) is the comparable record, and the percentages there have to agree with the register the applicant calls a cap table.


Consistency is the core check for this document type. Holder names, share counts, and certificate numbers on the register should match any stock certificates in the packet. Percentages should match the beneficial ownership certification. The owner on the register at 24 percent should not be the same person who signed the application as CEO with no other control person named. A generated register tends to be internally perfect and externally wrong, so inconsistency across documents fails and internal consistency alone passes nothing.


Model artifacts are what a generated table leaves: uniform row spacing no export produces, rounded percentages that do not divide from the share counts, and column labels that match no known platform or statute. Recycled patterns close serial reuse: one register template, one set of holder addresses, or one percentage split across applicants that claim no common owner. Those six checks are classes of evidence, not a recipe for a cleaner fake.


## What to Do with a Suspect File


Stop treating the upload as the register. Recompute every percentage from share counts on an issued-equity basis, then aggregate holders who share an address, a surname, an entity parent, or a signatory. If any person or related group reaches 25 percent, identify them as a beneficial owner and treat the certification as unreliable. 31 CFR 1010.230 lets an institution rely on customer-supplied ownership information only when it has no knowledge of facts that reasonably call that information into question. An arithmetic gap is such a fact.


Ask for the record from its keeper, not from the applicant's inbox. A native export sent by the cap-table administrator, the company secretary, or outside counsel is stronger than a PDF forwarded by the person being verified. Ask for transfer history covering any holder whose stake changed in the past year. A transfer that dropped someone from 30 to 24 percent just before onboarding is a question for the customer, and the answer goes in the file.


Apply the control prong regardless of what the percentages say. Identify the individual with significant responsibility to control, manage, or direct the entity, and check whether that person also appears on the register under a different name or through an entity.[UBO mapping](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/ubo-mapping-automation) across layered holdings is where a 24 percent direct stake turns into a 40 percent indirect one.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is a shareholder register?


A shareholder register is a company's record of its shareholders, the number and class of shares each holds, and when each became or ceased to be a holder. UK companies call it the register of members under section 113 of the Companies Act 2006. Delaware corporations call it the stock ledger under DGCL § 219.


### Is a cap table the same as a shareholder register?


No. A shareholder register records issued shares held by stockholders of record. A cap table is an ownership model that often includes options, warrants, and convertible instruments on a fully diluted basis. Percentages can differ between the two, so KYB reviewers should recompute ownership on issued equity before applying the 25 percent test.


### Why would someone fake a shareholder register?


The usual goal is to keep a person off the beneficial ownership list. Under 31 CFR 1010.230, individuals owning 25 percent or more of the equity must be identified, so an altered register may show an owner at 24 percent or split a stake across relatives and entities. The edit hides a person, not a company.


### Can someone below 25 percent still be a beneficial owner?


Yes. The CDD rule separately requires one individual with significant control, and FATF guidance says individuals who exercise ultimate control should be identified regardless of any ownership threshold. Related holders acting together can also be aggregated on a risk basis.


### How do you verify a shareholder register?


Recompute percentages from share counts, compare holders and classes to the articles, operating agreement, and any stock certificates, and request a native export directly from the company secretary, counsel, or cap-table administrator. Ask for transfer history behind any recent change near the 25 percent line, and run the file itself through a forensic check for edits made after creation.
